title: Ch3: Transport-Layer Services, Multiplexing and Demultiplexing

questions.q: The transport layer provides logical communication between which entities?
choices: Hosts (end systems) anywhere on the Internet
Application processes running on different hosts
Routers along the path between two hosts
Adjacent nodes on the same link
questions.explain: The transport layer provides process-to-process logical communication. Host-to-host communication is the network layer's job.

questions.q: What does it mean that two processes are connected by a "logical" channel at the transport layer?
choices: They must share a physical cable
Every router on the path keeps a record of their conversation
From the transport layer's point of view, sender and receiver behave as if they were directly connected, even though many networks, routers and links may separate them
The channel is guaranteed never to lose or reorder messages
questions.explain: The transport layer ignores everything between the two processes and only considers the properties of the channel that joins them. That channel can still lose, reorder or corrupt messages.

questions.q: The transport layer treats everything between the two communicating processes as one channel. What can this channel do to messages?
questions.explain: The underlying channel can lose, reorder or corrupt messages. Nothing promises a maximum delay. Delay guarantees are not available on the Internet at all.

questions.q: The sending transport layer breaks application messages into transport-layer packets and passes them to the network layer. What are these transport-layer packets called?
questions.explain: Sender: breaks application messages into segments and passes them to the network layer. Receiver: reassembles segments into messages and passes them to the application layer.

questions.q: Transport-protocol actions take place in the end systems (the sending and receiving hosts).
questions.explain: Transport protocols act in end systems. The sender breaks messages into segments, and the receiver reassembles them and passes them up to the application.

questions.q: Which of the following are transport-layer services?
choices: Moving datagrams from the source host to the destination host across many routers
questions.explain: Mux/demux, reliable data transfer, flow control and congestion control are transport-layer services. Carrying datagrams from host to host is the network layer's job (the postal service in the household analogy).

questions.q: Many senders adjust how fast they send so that their combined rate does not overwhelm or exhaust network resources. Which transport-layer service is this?
questions.explain: Congestion control is about a group of senders adjusting their sending rates so that their total load does not overwhelm the network.

questions.q: The network layer provides logical communication between:
questions.explain: Network layer = communication between hosts. Transport layer = communication between processes. This difference is the main split between the two layers.

questions.q: The transport layer relies on the network layer's services and can also enhance them.
questions.explain: The transport layer sits on top of the network layer. For example, UDP is a no-frills extension of best-effort IP, while TCP adds reliable, in-order delivery on top of it.

questions.q: In the household analogy (12 kids in Ann's house send letters to 12 kids in Bill's house), what does the postal service stand for?
questions.explain: The postal service only moves letters from one house to another (host to host), which is the network layer's job. What happens inside each house is the transport layer's job.

questions.q: In the household analogy, what do Ann and Bill stand for?
questions.explain: Ann and Bill collect letters from the kids in their own house and hand out arriving letters to them. That is the transport layer's job. Houses = hosts, kids = processes, letters in envelopes = application messages, postal service = network layer.

questions.q: In the household analogy, which mapping is correct?
choices: Hosts = the postal service, processes = Ann and Bill
questions.explain: Each host (house) runs many processes (kids). Application messages are the letters in envelopes.

questions.q: A letter arrives at Ann's house and Ann gives it to the right child. Which networking function does this correspond to?
questions.explain: Similarly, when a datagram arrives at a host, the host must deliver its contents to the right process. Doing that inside the host is transport-layer demultiplexing. The postal service (network layer) only gets the letter to the house.

questions.q: In what order does the sending transport layer act?
choices: Creates segment → determines segment header field values → is passed an application-layer message → passes segment to IP
Is passed an application-layer message → passes the message to IP → IP determines header fields → creates segment
Is passed an application-layer message → determines segment header field values → creates segment → passes segment to IP
Determines segment header field values → passes segment to IP → is passed an application-layer message → creates segment
questions.explain: The application writes a message into a socket. The transport layer then fills in the segment header values, builds the segment (header + app message), and hands it to IP, which delivers it to the receiving host.

questions.q: Which of the following are actions of the receiving transport layer?
choices: Demultiplexes the message up to the application via a socket
Determines the segment header field values
questions.explain: Determining header field values is a sender action. The receiver takes the segment from IP, checks the header, extracts the message and demultiplexes it to the correct socket.

questions.q: One reason the receiving transport layer checks a segment's header values is to:
choices: Choose the route the next segment will take
Make sure the segment has not been corrupted
Add a transport header for the network layer
Assign the sender a new IP address
questions.explain: The receiver checks header fields, for example to confirm that the segment was not corrupted, before it extracts the message and demultiplexes it.

questions.q: After building a segment, the sending transport layer passes it to:
choices: The network layer (IP, in the Internet)
The application process through its socket
The receiving host's transport layer directly
questions.explain: The segment goes down to IP. The network layer is responsible for delivering the IP datagram from the sending host to the receiving host.

questions.q: A slide shows a packet as "Hn Ht HTTP msg". Which statement is correct?
choices: Hn is the transport header and Ht is the network-layer header
Ht is the transport-layer header, and Hn is the network-layer header placed in front of the segment
Both Hn and Ht are parts of the HTTP application message
Ht is added by the receiving host's transport layer
questions.explain: The sending transport layer adds Ht to the HTTP message to form a segment. The network layer then adds Hn to form a datagram. The receiver removes them in reverse order.

questions.q: Which services does TCP provide?
questions.explain: TCP: reliable in-order delivery, congestion control, flow control, connection setup. No Internet transport protocol provides delay or bandwidth guarantees.

questions.q: Which description best fits UDP?
choices: Reliable, connection-oriented transport with congestion control
Reliable delivery, but with no ordering guarantee
Guaranteed bandwidth with no connection setup
Unreliable, unordered delivery; a no-frills extension of best-effort IP
questions.explain: UDP is a connectionless, best-effort service: delivery is unreliable and unordered, and it adds very little on top of IP.

questions.q: Which services are NOT available from either TCP or UDP?
questions.explain: TCP provides reliable in-order delivery and congestion control. Neither Internet transport protocol guarantees delay or bandwidth.

questions.q: An interactive voice (phone call) application wants a guaranteed upper bound on the time between writing a message into a socket and its arrival at the other end. Which Internet transport protocol offers this?
questions.explain: Delay guarantees would be valuable for interactive voice, but no Internet transport protocol provides them.

questions.q: A streaming-video service wants a guaranteed rate, in megabits per second, between sender and receiver. What kind of service is this, and does the Internet transport layer provide it?
choices: A bandwidth guarantee; provided by neither TCP nor UDP
A bandwidth guarantee; provided by TCP's congestion control
A delay guarantee; provided by UDP
Reliable data transfer; provided by TCP
questions.explain: A guaranteed throughput between sender and receiver is a bandwidth guarantee. Like delay guarantees, it is not available from TCP or UDP.

questions.q: What does the acronym TCP stand for?
questions.explain: TCP = Transmission Control Protocol: the Internet's reliable, connection-oriented transport protocol.

questions.q: What does the acronym UDP stand for?
questions.explain: UDP = User Datagram Protocol: the Internet's connectionless, best-effort transport protocol.

questions.q: To provide reliability, flow control and congestion control, TCP sets up a connection and keeps connection state at both the sender and the receiver.
questions.explain: TCP's reliability, flow control and congestion control need connection state on both sides, so TCP sets up a connection first.

questions.q: UDP guarantees that messages arrive in the order they were sent.
questions.explain: UDP delivery is unreliable and unordered. Messages may be lost or arrive out of order.

questions.q: What is demultiplexing at the receiving host?
choices: Collecting data from several sockets and adding transport headers
Choosing the route a datagram takes through the network
Using header information to deliver received segments to the correct socket
Splitting a large message into several segments
questions.explain: Demultiplexing (receiver) uses header info to deliver each received segment to the correct socket. Collecting data from sockets and adding headers is multiplexing (sender).

questions.q: What is multiplexing at the sending host?
choices: Handling data from multiple sockets and adding a transport header, which is later used for demultiplexing
Using header information to pick the socket for an arriving segment
Sending the same segment to many destination hosts at once
Combining several segments into one IP datagram
questions.explain: The sender's transport layer gathers data from many sockets into segments and passes them down to the network layer. The header it adds carries the information the receiver needs for demultiplexing. Note that each IP datagram carries only one segment.

questions.q: Multiplexing and demultiplexing happen only at the transport layer.
questions.explain: Multiplexing and demultiplexing happen at all layers of the protocol stack. They come up again at the network and link layers.

questions.q: Demultiplexing in a host can direct an arriving payload to one of several protocols running in that host, not only to one of several applications.
questions.explain: Payloads arriving at a host may be headed for different applications or for different protocols running in that host. Sending each one to the right place is demultiplexing.

questions.q: When a host receives an IP datagram, which values can it use to send the segment inside to the appropriate socket?
choices: The name of the destination application (e.g., "firefox")
questions.explain: The host uses IP addresses and port numbers to direct segments to sockets. The headers don't carry application names. Which of these values are actually used depends on the protocol: UDP uses the destination port only, TCP uses all four.

questions.q: Where are the source and destination port numbers carried?
choices: In the IP datagram header, next to the IP addresses
Only in the sockets; they are never sent
questions.explain: The IP datagram carries the source and destination IP addresses. The segment it carries has source and destination port numbers as the first fields of its header.

questions.q: In the TCP/UDP segment format, the first 32-bit row of the header holds the source port # and the destination port # side by side, each filling half the row. How many bits is each port number field?
questions.explain: 32 bits split evenly between the two fields gives 16 bits each.

questions.q: Each IP datagram carries one transport-layer segment.
questions.explain: Each datagram has source and destination IP addresses and carries exactly one transport-layer segment, which has source and destination port numbers.

questions.q: At an airport, business-class passengers are sent one way and economy another, and TSA PreCheck passengers go to a separate line. Which concept does this splitting and directing illustrate?
questions.explain: Splitting one incoming stream and directing each item to its own class of service is demultiplexing. Highway exit ramps are another example. On-ramps merging cars onto a highway are an example of multiplexing.

questions.q: Cars from several on-ramps merging onto a single highway best illustrate:
questions.explain: Many inputs funneled into one shared path is multiplexing, just like many sockets' data going down through the transport layer into IP.

questions.q: A client is running Skype, Netflix and Firefox when an HTTP reply arrives from a web server. How does the client's transport layer know to deliver the message to Firefox?
choices: It reads the HTTP message to see which application requested it
It uses the segment's header information (port numbers, plus IP addresses) to identify Firefox's socket
The network layer hands the message directly to Firefox
It delivers a copy to every application and lets each one decide
questions.explain: Demultiplexing uses header field values, not application data. The port numbers (with the IP addresses, for TCP) identify the socket that belongs to the browser.

questions.q: Which field(s) does a receiving host use to demultiplex a UDP segment to a socket?
choices: Source IP address and source port number
All four: source/destination IP addresses and source/destination port numbers
questions.explain: UDP demultiplexing checks the destination port number and directs the segment to the socket that has that port number. TCP is the protocol that uses the full 4-tuple.

questions.q: Two UDP datagrams arrive at a host with the same destination port number but different source IP addresses and different source port numbers. They are delivered to the same socket.
questions.explain: UDP demultiplexes on the destination port number only. Datagrams with the same destination port go to the same socket, wherever they came from.

questions.q: In the code `DatagramSocket mySocket1 = new DatagramSocket(12534);`, what is 12534?
choices: The destination port number of the remote host
The host-local port number of the new socket
questions.explain: When you create a UDP socket you must give it a host-local port number. Arriving UDP segments whose destination port is 12534 are delivered to this socket.

questions.q: When a program creates a datagram to send into a UDP socket, what must it specify?
choices: A connection identifier obtained from a handshake
The remote host's source port number
questions.explain: Every UDP datagram must name its destination IP address and destination port number. UDP is connectionless, so there is no handshake and no connection identifier.

questions.q: Process P3 has a UDP socket bound to port 9157 and sends a datagram to process P1, whose UDP socket is bound to port 6428. P1 replies to P3. What port numbers does the reply carry?
questions.explain: The original datagram has source 9157 and dest 6428. In the reply the two are swapped: P1's socket port 6428 becomes the source, and the destination 9157 comes from the source port of the datagram being answered.

questions.q: Process P4 has a UDP socket bound to port 5775 and sends a datagram to process P1, whose UDP socket is bound to port 6428. What destination port number does P4's datagram carry?
questions.explain: The destination port is the port of the receiving socket (P1's, 6428). The source port is P4's own socket port, 5775.

questions.q: Continuing: P1 (UDP port 6428) replies to the datagram from P4 (UDP port 5775). What destination port number does P1's reply carry?
questions.explain: The reply goes back to P4's socket, so its destination port is 5775, taken from the source port of the arriving datagram. Its source port is 6428.

questions.q: When a UDP process replies to a datagram it received, where does the reply's destination port number come from?
choices: It is always the same as the replying process's own local port
It is chosen at random by the transport layer
From the source port number of the arriving datagram being replied to
From the network layer's routing table
questions.explain: The source port of the arriving datagram identifies the sender's socket, so the reply uses it as its destination port.

questions.q: A server has a UDP socket bound to port 5000. Host X and host Y (different IP addresses) each send datagrams to the server's port 5000, both from source port 3000. How many sockets at the server receive these datagrams?
questions.explain: UDP demultiplexes on the destination port only. Every datagram has destination port 5000, so they all go to the same socket.

questions.q: A TCP socket is identified by a 4-tuple. Which values make up that 4-tuple?
questions.explain: 4-tuple = (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). The receiver uses all four values to direct a segment to the right socket.

questions.q: A TCP server can support many simultaneous TCP sockets, each identified by its own 4-tuple and each associated with a different connecting client.
questions.explain: Because sockets are told apart by the full 4-tuple, a server can keep one socket per connecting client, even when they all use the same server port.

questions.q: Web server B receives three TCP segments, all with destination IP B and destination port 80: one from (A, port 9157), one from (C, port 5775), and one from (C, port 9157). Into how many different sockets are they demultiplexed?
questions.explain: Each segment has a different 4-tuple, so each one goes to its own socket, even though all three share the destination IP B and port 80.

questions.q: Two TCP segments arrive at server B, port 80. One comes from host A, port 9157; the other comes from host C, also port 9157. Why are they delivered to different sockets?
choices: TCP demultiplexes on the 4-tuple, and the two source IP addresses differ
TCP demultiplexes on the destination port only and assigns sockets round-robin
They are not; TCP delivers them to the same socket because the ports match
TCP compares the application data inside the segments
questions.explain: The source ports and the destination (B, 80) are the same, but the source IPs (A and C) differ. That makes the 4-tuples different, so the segments go to different sockets.

questions.q: Suppose the three segments from (A, 9157), (C, 5775) and (C, 9157) were instead UDP datagrams sent to a single UDP socket bound to port 80 at server B. Where would they be delivered?
choices: To two sockets: one for host A and one for host C
They would be dropped because the source ports repeat
questions.explain: UDP demultiplexes on the destination port only. All three have destination port 80, so all go to the same socket. This is the main difference from TCP's 4-tuple demultiplexing.

questions.q: Web server B (port 80) sends a reply to client A, whose TCP socket uses port 9157. What are the reply's source and destination (IP, port)?
questions.explain: The reply reverses the client's segment, which had source (A, 9157) and destination (B, 80).

questions.q: For TCP, the receiver uses only the destination port number to choose the socket.
questions.explain: Destination-port-only demultiplexing is UDP's method. TCP is connection-oriented and uses all four values of the 4-tuple.

questions.q: Why can't a busy TCP web server demultiplex on the destination port number alone?
choices: Port number fields are too short to identify a server
Many clients connect to the same server port (e.g., 80), and each connection has its own socket, so the source IP and port are needed to tell the connections apart
TCP segments do not carry a destination port number
The destination port number changes with every segment
questions.explain: All the clients' segments have the same destination port (80). Only the source IP address and source port differ, so TCP needs the full 4-tuple to find each connection's socket.
